title: Project 4: file-based expense tracker
learningObjectives: Design a simple text-file record format for an expense date, category and amount.
Explain how fopen, fgets, fprintf, ferror and fclose are used to manage a text file.
Validate calendar dates, bounded category text and positive monetary amounts.
Represent money as integer cents to avoid binary floating-point rounding in totals.
Append expense records, read existing records and calculate a total with overflow checks.
Handle missing files, malformed records, overlong lines and file I/O errors without treating invalid data as valid.

understand.concept: A file-based expense tracker stores one expense per line so records remain available after the program exits. Each record contains a date in YYYY-MM-DD form, a category and an amount. This project uses a documented pipe-delimited text format: date|category|cents. The amount is stored as a positive integer number of cents, not as a floating-point value. For example, 125.50 is stored as 12550. The program appends new records, reads the file back, validates each line and adds valid amounts to a running total.
understand.whyItMatters: Persistent data is a core requirement in practical programs. This project combines structures, text parsing, file streams, input validation, error reporting and arithmetic while making the file format explicit and inspectable.
understand.analogy: Think of the file as a paper ledger: each line is one expense entry, and the total is calculated by adding the valid entries.
understand.analogyLimit: A text file does not enforce a schema or protect itself from damaged lines. The C program must validate the format, check every file operation and decide how to handle invalid records.

explain.narrative:
The file format used here is one record per line: YYYY-MM-DD|category|cents. The date has exactly ten characters and is checked as a real calendar date, including leap years. A category is non-empty, bounded and cannot contain the pipe delimiter or control characters. The amount is a positive integer count of cents. A display amount such as 49.95 is converted to 4995 cents before storage. Keeping money in integer cents avoids common floating-point representation surprises when adding currency values.

Use fopen with mode a to append and mode r to read. Always check whether fopen returned NULL. Check fprintf for a negative result and check fclose for EOF because buffered write errors can be reported when the stream is closed. While reading, use fgets with a fixed-size buffer. Detect a line that does not fit, discard the rest of that line and count it as invalid rather than parsing a partial record. Check ferror after the read loop and check fclose.

A file may contain malformed or manually edited lines. Parse each record into a temporary structure and only use it after all fields pass validation. This implementation skips invalid lines and reports how many were skipped. If no file exists yet, listing reports that there are no saved expenses. The running total is checked against LLONG_MAX before addition so signed overflow is avoided.

The examples are intentionally small and use a local text file named expenses.txt. They do not provide encryption, multi-user locking, backups or transactional crash recovery. Those are separate production concerns. The file is a plain-text teaching format, so do not store sensitive personal or payment information in it.

examples.title: Validate expense records and calculate a safe total
examples.explanation: This deterministic test program validates leap-year dates, category and delimiter rules, positive integer-cent amounts and malformed lines. It also checks that a running total refuses an addition that would overflow a long long. The tests do not depend on an external file, so they can run repeatedly with the same result.

examples.title: Complete append, list and total expense tracker
examples.explanation: The interactive program appends records to expenses.txt, reads them back, skips malformed or overlong lines, and displays a total using integer cents. It checks file opening, writes, read errors and close errors. Enter dates as YYYY-MM-DD, categories without the pipe character, and amounts with at most two decimal places.

practise.guidedTask: Run the deterministic tests and trace how 1250 cents plus 250 cents becomes a total of 1500 cents. Open the generated text file after adding an expense and explain why the amount is stored as an integer number of cents.
practise.independentTask: Extend the tracker with a category summary that totals valid expenses per category. Reuse the existing record parser, reject malformed records, check every total addition for overflow and test a missing file, an empty file, leap-day dates, invalid dates, amounts with zero/one/two decimal places, excessive decimal places, a category containing the delimiter, an overlong line and a failed file-open scenario. Keep the file format documented and do not use floating-point values for money.
hints: Write down the exact record format before implementing either the writer or the parser.
Store currency as integer cents and convert to a display value only when printing.
Validate a complete record in a temporary structure before including it in the total.
Use append mode to add records without replacing earlier entries, and check fopen, fprintf and fclose.
When fgets does not capture a complete line, discard the remainder so the next read starts at a record boundary.
Before adding a positive amount to a total, check that the addition cannot exceed LLONG_MAX.

questions.prompt: Why does this project store an expense amount as integer cents?
options: To avoid common floating-point rounding surprises in currency totals.
Because C cannot store decimal values.
To make every expense amount negative.
questions.answer: To avoid common floating-point rounding surprises in currency totals.
questions.explanation: Integer cents represent the smallest unit used by this example and make addition exact as long as overflow is checked.

questions.prompt: Which fopen mode appends new records while preserving existing file contents?
questions.explanation: Append mode writes new data at the end of the file and creates the file if it does not exist.

questions.prompt: What should a program do when fopen returns NULL?
options: Report or handle the open failure and avoid using the stream.
Continue calling fprintf with the null pointer.
Assume the file is empty in every case.
questions.answer: Report or handle the open failure and avoid using the stream.
questions.explanation: A NULL FILE pointer means the stream was not opened and cannot be used for file I/O.

questions.prompt: Why should each line be parsed and validated before its amount is added to the total?
options: A text file may contain malformed or manually edited records.
fgets guarantees that every line follows the expected format.
Invalid lines should always be treated as zero-valued expenses.
questions.answer: A text file may contain malformed or manually edited records.
questions.explanation: Validation prevents partial, malformed or out-of-range data from silently affecting the result.

questions.prompt: Which check helps prevent signed overflow when adding positive cents to a total?
options: Verify total is no greater than LLONG_MAX minus the new amount.
Add first and check whether the result wrapped around.
Convert the total to unsigned and ignore the original range.
questions.answer: Verify total is no greater than LLONG_MAX minus the new amount.
questions.explanation: Checking the remaining representable range before addition avoids executing an overflowing signed operation.
